summary: Customer asked detailed questions about what admin events Redwood captures, how exported logs can be encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, and options for short-term telemetry vs long-term archive. We agreed to run a 24h snapshot of admin activity, provide concrete export scripts using S3 + KMS envelope, and follow up with a POC kickoff to onboard a customer-managed key and test retention/restore flows.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-06-11
- Start: 15:30 UTC
- Duration: ~57 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Anika Patel (Redwood SE), Luis Moreno (Redwood CR), Sonia Rhee (Mercator Head of Security), Tomás Alvarez (Infra), Priya Shah (Compliance), Ethan Cole (Platform)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick compliance sync focused on admin-event capture, exports, and KMS integration.

[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off, Sonia thanks for setting aside time. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Sonia Rhee: Hi, Sonia here. We got Tomás, Priya, Ethan on the call as well.
[00:18] Jordan Park: Great — I can do a 2 minute framing, Anika will deep dive on the export and key management flow, and then we'll open up for specifics.
[00:29] Tomás Alvarez: Sounds good. Main thing for us is to understand exactly what "admin events" means in your schema and what can be exported off-platform for our SIEM.
[00:37] Anika Patel: Perfect. So at a high level Redwood captures admin activity at multiple layers: control-plane actions (role changes, API key lifecycle, SSO events), runtime admin events (instance scale, model pin/unpin, deployment rollouts), and operational telemetry (errors, retries).
[00:52] Ethan Cole: When you say SSO events — we're using Okta, we need to capture SAML assertions and successful logins plus failed auth attempts, right?
[01:01] Anika Patel: We capture the event types: SAML_LOGIN_SUCCESS, SAML_LOGIN_FAILURE, SAML_TOKEN_REFRESH. We don't store full assertions by default but we capture enough context (user id, timestamp, IP, reason). If you need raw assertion artifacts we can discuss a different retention model — they contain PII.
[01:18] Priya Shah: For auditability, we need immutable records and hash chaining for evidence. Do you provide integrity controls on exported files?
[01:26] Luis Moreno: Right now export bundles include a manifest and we can sign manifests. For customer-managed keys we suggest envelope encryption so the object is encrypted with a data key and that data key is wrapped by the customer's KMS. The manifest also includes SHA256 checksums for each file so you can validate after transfer.
[01:45] Sonia Rhee: Okay that piece is critical. Also we have to ensure logs stored outside the EU are not accidentally replicated — data residency controls.
[01:54] Anika Patel: We support routing by region and can export to a region-specific S3 bucket (we create pre-signed upload destination or push to your bucket). You can pin exports to eu-west-1 or europe-west-1, whichever you use. We'll show the configuration.
[02:09] Tomás Alvarez: About retention — we do 7 years for forensics but we plan to tier older logs to offline cold storage. How does Redwood handle retention policies and deletions?
[02:18] Jordan Park: There are two layers. On-platform retention — how long telemetry remains in Redwood for search/console access — and exported retention — what you keep in your archive. On-platform you can set retention per resource and event type (e.g., admin events 90 days). For long term, we recommend exporting nightly and then lifecycle rules in your archive (S3 GLACIER) for 7-year cold retention.
[02:39] Sonia Rhee: Are exports atomic? If we run an export job and it fails mid-stream, do you provide resumable delivery?
[02:46] Anika Patel: Exports are chunked and each chunk has a manifest entry. We support resumable uploads to S3 via multi-part and we also keep a server-side export cursor so we can retry the chunk generation without duplicating events.
[02:59] Ethan Cole: On the key management front — we run a customer-managed KMS in Azure Key Vault. Can you do envelope encryption with CMK where we retain key control and you never see plaintext?
[03:09] Anika Patel: Yes. We support envelope encryption patterns: Redwood will generate a data key to encrypt the object, wrap that data key with your CMK, and only store the wrapped key. We never persist the unwrapped key. For Azure we can integrate with Key Vault using a transient key wrap/unwrapping flow during exports. We also support AWS KMS and Google KMS.
[03:28] Tomás Alvarez: Is the wrapped key rotatable? We rotate CMKs quarterly.
[03:34] Luis Moreno: Rotation is fine — when a key rotates, your KMS will still be able to unwrap older wrapped data keys as long as the appropriate key policy and key versions are retained. For extreme cases we can export wrapped-key material in a key-archive so you can rewrap after rotation if needed.
[03:51] Priya Shah: For compliance, we need retention proof and deletion logs. If Redwood deletes a log row or an exported bundle is expired, do you provide evidence of deletion?
[04:01] Anika Patel: We can provide deletion audit events which include deletion timestamp, actor, and deletion reason. For exported objects, lifecycle events are emitted when we trigger retention purge and those are included in the manifest.
[04:15] Sonia Rhee: How granular is RBAC metadata in the logs? We need to tie actions to group membership at time of action.
[04:23] Anika Patel: Each admin event includes actor id, actor type (user, service), the effective principal (groups) — although group names are based on your SSO mapping at event time. There can be drift if group membership changes later; we snapshot group membership at the time of the event to provide historical context.
[04:39] Tomás Alvarez: That snapshotting is good. Can you also include the policy version applied at the time of the action?
[04:45] Anika Patel: Yes, we include policy_version when relevant for authorization events.
[04:49] Ethan Cole: A practical question — we use an internal ELK cluster. Can Redwood push logs to a collector endpoint or do you require pull from S3?
[04:58] Anika Patel: Both. We offer push via secure HTTPS webhook to an endpoint you provide (mutual TLS supported) and we also provide S3 exports for batch/archival. For high volume near-real-time integration we'd usually recommend our streaming connector to a Kinesis/IoT or to push to your collector. There's a throughput tradeoff and cost consideration which we'll layout.
[05:22] Sonia Rhee: If we use push, how do you guarantee delivery ordering / de-duplication?
[05:28] Anika Patel: Events have monotonic sequence IDs per tenant. Our client library can use those to dedupe. With HTTPS push we also support an ack-based flow and will retry on 5xx.
[05:39] Tomás Alvarez: For the POC we want to try: 1) 24h admin-event snapshot exported to our EU S3 bucket with envelope encryption via our CMK; 2) streaming of SSO failures to our SIEM for alerting. Is that doable?
[05:52] Jordan Park: Absolutely — that's exactly the type of POC we recommend. We'll provide an export config and Anika will help on key onboarding.
[06:00] Sonia Rhee: One more question on logs — do you capture changes to RBAC policies via API and console separately? We need to show who changed what and whether the change came from UI or API.
[06:09] Anika Patel: We capture event origin: UI, API token, terraform provider. The event includes source (ui/api/infra) and metadata like IP and user agent string if available.
[06:19] Priya Shah: About retention labels — we label events with classification (admin, billing, content). Can we map Redwood labels to our internal retention categories so downstream tooling can pick correct lifecycles?
[06:30] Luis Moreno: Yes, export manifests contain event classification and you can request custom tags during the export pipeline, we'll inject customer_tag metadata.
[06:40] Tomás Alvarez: On the subject of audits, we will be asking for a weekly digest of anomalous admin actions. Do you have out-of-the-box anomaly scoring?
[06:49] Anika Patel: We have basic heuristics for anomaly detection (spike in failed logins, unusual IPs, privilege escalation events). For POC we'll share a simple rule set you can run in your SIEM, or we can stream anomalies as higher-priority events.
[07:02] Sonia Rhee: Ok that helps. Could you also confirm data minimization — like are IP addresses truncated by default or full?
[07:09] Anika Patel: We store full IPs in the admin event by default for forensic value. If you have a stricter privacy requirement we can support truncation or hashing at ingest. Note that truncation makes certain forensic tasks harder.
[07:21] Ethan Cole: Regarding format, what schema do events follow? JSON lines, Avro, protobuf?
[07:27] Anika Patel: Exports default to JSONL with a typed schema version (admin_v2). We can also produce Avro for more compact archives. We'll attach the schema to the manifest.
[07:37] Tomás Alvarez: For the envelope encryption example, can you walk us quickly through the flow?
[07:41] Anika Patel: Sure — flow is: 1) Redwood generates a one-time data key (DEK) 2) DEK encrypts the object 3) Redwood requests your KMS to wrap the DEK and receives wrapped key blob 4) Redwood stores only the wrapped key alongside the encrypted object 5) On your side, to decrypt, you retrieve the object and ask KMS to unwrap the DEK. That way Redwood never has unwrapped key.
[08:05] Tomás Alvarez: For Azure Key Vault, do you support managed identities or will we need to provision credentials?
[08:12] Anika Patel: We support both. For non-interactive flows we can use a service principal with limited permissions or managed identity if you host the on-prem connector in your subscription. We'll send the exact permission set needed.
[08:23] Sonia Rhee: Are there limits on export frequency / rate?
[08:27] Luis Moreno: For large customers we often provision a reserved export throughput. For ad-hoc exports you can run nightly or on-demand; heavy streaming will hit throughput limits and we size it per contract. We'll propose default rate limits in the POC doc.
[08:41] Priya Shah: We're also concerned about forensic continuity — if Redwood is down can we still retrieve logs?
[08:47] Jordan Park: Short answer: if logs were exported previously you still control them in your archive. If Redwood is entirely down and you hadn't exported, we have retention backups for a short window as part of our SLA but that's not a long-term plan. The mitigation is frequent or continuous exports.
[09:02] Ethan Cole: Can you produce a tamper-evidence chain beyond checksums — e.g., sign manifests with an asymmetric key?
[09:10] Anika Patel: Yes, we can sign manifests with an RSA/ECDSA key and ship the public key for verification. For higher assurance we support time-stamped signatures via an external TSA if required.
[09:22] Sonia Rhee: Ok, let's talk threats — things we worry about: leaked API keys, rogue admin, accidental deletion. Show me detection and rollback story.
[09:32] Anika Patel: Detection: we emit immediate admin events on API key creation, API key usage anomalies, and privilege changes. For rollback: we have snapshot-based restores for config state — you can pin a model config and rollback. For deeper remediation we provide a playbook with recommended steps (revoke keys, rotate CMK if you think wrapped keys are impacted, restore state from snapshot).
[09:50] Tomás Alvarez: If a key is compromised, will rotating the CMK prevent decrypting old archives?
[09:56] Luis Moreno: Rotation by itself doesn't prevent unwrapping if you retain old key versions. If you retire a key and delete old key versions per your KMS policy then you will lose ability to unwrap older data. Make sure your key rotation policy retains history long enough for your archives.
[10:11] Jordan Park: Alright folks, we're at about 10 minutes into the call recorded header but the transcript continues — skipping forward to wrap up action items and the POC scope.
[10:22] Anika Patel: For the POC scope we'll do: a) 24h admin event dump to your EU S3 with envelope encryption b) streaming alerts for SSO failures to your SIEM via mutual-TLS push c) provide schema + manifest signing d) run a restore exercise to validate decryption and tamper checks.
[10:42] Sonia Rhee: That matches our ask. On the restore exercise, we want a proof of deletion as well: after we delete an export we'll request evidence that it's been removed from Redwood and our staging bucket (if Redwood wrote a temp) — basically a chain of custody.
[10:58] Anika Patel: We'll include deletion manifests and signed deletion receipts for that flow.
[11:05] Tomás Alvarez: Any blockers on our side? We'll need to provision an S3 bucket with correct KMS policy and a service principal for Azure key wrap testing.
[11:13] Jordan Park: Sounds reasonable. We'll attach a runbook for the pre-reqs in the POC doc.
[11:20] Priya Shah: On the SOC2 and ISO front, can you point us to the evidence items we should expect?
[11:26] Jordan Park: We'll send an evidence pack: SOC 2 Type II report summary, control mappings, relevant audit log retention and integrity controls, plus the admin-event schema and sampling.
[11:36] Sonia Rhee: Do you have a public hardening guide for the on-prem connector?
[11:40] Anika Patel: Yes, we have a hardening guide. We'll share it — includes recommended network rules, mTLS setup, least-priv permissions for service principals.
[11:49] Ethan Cole: Quick nit: you mentioned "KV cache" earlier in some docs — what is that in the export context?
[11:55] Anika Patel: That's a runtime artifact for inference caching; it doesn't contain admin events. A doc mismatch there — sorry. The K-V cache is not part of admin telemetry exports.
[12:06] Tomás Alvarez: Good to clear.
[12:08] Jordan Park: Alright, wrapping — we'll deliver the POC proposal and sample scripts, and Mercator will stand up the EU S3 and the service principal.
[12:18] Sonia Rhee: Thanks everyone. We'll expect the docs from Jordan and Anika.
[12:22] Jordan Park: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the POC kickoff.

Recap / Close: Action items captured in recording. Meeting ends.

Notes on transcription artifacts: occasional mis-heard phrases (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache, timestamps approximate), some speaker overlaps.
